claim: CD95/Fas ligand binds to the death receptor CD95 to induce apoptosis in sensitive cells.
source: CD95/Fas ligand binds to the death receptor CD95 to induce apoptosis in sensitive cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citation to Suda et al., 1993 in the Introduction.

claim: CD95L mRNA is enriched in sequences that, when converted to si/shRNAs, kill all cancer cells by targeting critical survival genes.
source: We previously reported that CD95L mRNA is enriched in sequences that, when converted to si/shRNAs, kill all cancer cells by targeting critical survival genes (Putzbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors (Putzbach et al., 2017).

claim: Expression of full-length CD95L mRNA itself is highly toxic to cells.
source: We now report expression of full-length CD95L mRNA itself is highly toxic to cells and induces a similar form of cell death.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-2.

claim: Small RNAs derived from CD95L are loaded into the RNA induced silencing complex (RISC).
source: We demonstrate that small (s)RNAs derived from CD95L are loaded into the RNA induced silencing complex (RISC) which is required for the toxicity
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Ago pull-down experiments shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: The RISC is required for the toxicity of CD95L mRNA.
source: We demonstrate that small (s)RNAs derived from CD95L are loaded into the RNA induced silencing complex (RISC) which is required for the toxicity
evidence: This is supported by AGO2 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Processing of CD95L mRNA into sRNAs is independent of both Dicer and Drosha.
source: processing of CD95L mRNA into sRNAs is independent of both Dicer and Drosha.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in Dicer and Drosha knockout cells shown in Figure 3A and Figure 4F-G.

claim: Endogenous protein coding genes involved in regulating protein translation can be processed to sRNAs and loaded into the RISC.
source: We provide evidence that in addition to the CD95L transgene a number of endogenous protein coding genes involved in regulating protein translation, particularly under low miRNA conditions, can be processed to sRNAs and loaded into the RISC
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of Ago-bound RNAs shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplements.

claim: The toxicity of CD95L mRNA is independent of the full-length CD95L protein.
source: This toxicity is independent of the full-length CD95L protein or expression of the CD95 receptor and resembles DISE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments using CD95L mutants that cannot bind CD95 and in CD95 knockout cells, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The toxicity of CD95L mRNA is independent of CD95 receptor expression.
source: This toxicity is independent of the full-length CD95L protein or expression of the CD95 receptor and resembles DISE.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in CD95 knockout cells shown in Figure 1A (right panel) and Figure 1E.

claim: CD95L mRNA-induced cell death resembles DISE (Death Induced by Survival gene Elimination).
source: This toxicity is independent of the full-length CD95L protein or expression of the CD95 receptor and resembles DISE.
evidence: This is supported by morphological observations (Figure 2A), gene expression analysis (Figure 2B-D), and ROS production (Figure 1D).

claim: Virtually all research on CD95 and CD95L has focused on the physical interaction between the two proteins and subsequent protein-based signaling cascades.
source: Virtually all research on CD95 and CD95L has focused on the physical interaction between the two proteins and the subsequent protein-based signaling cascades (Algeciras-Schimnich et al., 2002; Fu et al., 2016; Nisihara et al., 2001; Schneider et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mRNA of CD95 and CD95L harbor sequences that when converted into si/shRNAs cause massive and robust toxicity in all tested cancer cells.
source: However, we have recently shown that the mRNA of CD95 and CD95L harbor sequences that when converted into small interfering (si) or short hairpin (sh)RNAs, cause massive and robust toxicity in all tested cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Putzbach et al., 2017).

claim: CD95/CD95L-derived si/shRNAs target a network of survival genes, resulting in simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways through RNA interference.
source: These CD95/CD95L-derived si/shRNAs target a network of survival genes, resulting in the simultaneous activation of multiple cell death pathways through RNA interference (RNAi) in a process we called DISE (Death Induced by Survival gene Elimination) (Putzbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Putzbach et al., 2017).

claim: For a si/shRNA to elicit DISE toxicity, only positions 2–7 of the guide strand (the 6mer seed sequence) are required.
source: We determined that for a si/shRNA to elicit this form of toxicity, only positions 2–7 of the guide strand, the 6mer seed sequence, are required (Putzbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Putzbach et al., 2017).

claim: Optimal 6mer seed toxicity requires G-rich seeds targeting C-rich regions in the 3'UTRs of survival genes.
source: More recently, a screen of all 4096 6mer seeds revealed that optimal 6mer seed toxicity requires G-rich seeds targeting C-rich regions in the 3'UTRs of survival genes (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gao et al., 2018).

claim: Multiple sRNAs are generated from the mRNA of CD95L within cells.
source: We found that multiple sRNAs are generated from the mRNA of CD95L within cells and are loaded into the RNA-induced Silencing Complex (RISC), the key mediator of RNAi (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4B-E.

claim: The RISC is the key mediator of RNAi.
source: We found that multiple sRNAs are generated from the mRNA of CD95L within cells and are loaded into the RNA-induced Silencing Complex (RISC), the key mediator of RNAi (Liu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Liu et al., 2004.

claim: Endogenous mRNAs can be processed into sRNAs and loaded into the RISC, especially in cells with low expression of miRNAs.
source: Furthermore, we provide evidence that endogenous mRNAs can be processed into sRNAs and loaded into the RISC, especially in cells with low expression of miRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis in Drosha knockout cells shown in Figure 5.

claim: The subset of genes found in the RISC are regulators of protein translation and cell proliferation.
source: The subset of genes found in the RISC are regulators of protein translation and cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There is a high enrichment of toxic si/shRNAs derived from the CD95L ORF.
source: By testing every possible shRNA derived from the CD95L open reading frame (ORF) or its 3'UTR, we recently found a high enrichment of toxic si/shRNAs derived from the CD95L ORF (Putzbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Putzbach et al., 2017).

claim: The 6mer seed toxicity observed in many si/shRNAs is largely due to their nucleotide composition, with G-rich seeds being the most toxic.
source: More recently we determined that the 6mer seed toxicity observed in many si/shRNAs is largely due to their nucleotide composition, with G-rich seeds being the most toxic (Gao et al., 2018) (https://6merdb.org).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gao et al., 2018).

claim: There is a significant correlation between the toxicity of the most toxic CD95L-derived shRNAs and the toxicity of the corresponding 6mer seed.
source: When reanalyzing the CD95L ORF-derived shRNAs, we found a significant correlation between the toxicity of the most toxic CD95L-derived shRNAs (Putzbach et al., 2017) and the toxicity of the corresponding 6mer seed we recently determined in a screen of all 4096 6mer seeds (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of prior data from Putzbach et al., 2017 and Gao et al., 2018.

claim: CD95L-derived si/shRNAs kill cancer cells, in large part through 6mer seed toxicity.
source: This suggests that CD95L-derived si/shRNAs kill cancer cells, in large part through 6mer seed toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis mentioned in the previous claim.

claim: Expression of CD95L protein in most cells kills through the induction of apoptosis.
source: Expression of CD95L protein in most cells kills through the induction of apoptosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Expressing CD95L in HeyA8 cells, which are highly sensitive to CD95 mediated apoptosis, killed cells within a few hours after infection with a lentivirus encoding CD95L.
source: Consequently, expressing CD95L in HeyA8 cells, which are highly sensitive to CD95 mediated apoptosis, killed cells within a few hours after infection with a lentivirus encoding CD95L (Figure 1A, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, left panel.

claim: Severe growth reduction was seen without any signs of apoptosis when a CD95L mutant unable to bind CD95 was expressed.
source: Interestingly, severe growth reduction was seen without any signs of apoptosis (not shown) when a CD95L mutant, unable to bind CD95, was expressed (CD95LMUT in Figure 1A, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, left panel.

claim: The CD95LMUT mutant carries a Y218R point mutation that prevents the CD95L protein from binding to CD95.
source: This mutant carries an Y218R point mutation, that prevents the CD95L protein from binding to CD95 (Schneider et al., 1997), and is expressed at a similar level to wild type (wt) CD95L (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schneider et al., 1997 and Western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: CD95LMUT is expressed at a similar level to wild type CD95L.
source: This mutant carries an Y218R point mutation, that prevents the CD95L protein from binding to CD95 (Schneider et al., 1997), and is expressed at a similar level to wild type (wt) CD95L (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The CD95LMUTNP construct contains four point mutations and produces mRNA with no detectable full-length CD95L protein.
source: This construct (containing four point mutations and confirmed to produce mRNA with no detectable full-length CD95L protein, Figure 1B) was similarly active in reducing the growth of HeyA8 cells compared to the CD95LMUT vector (Figure 1A, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B showing no full-length protein.

claim: CD95LMUTNP was similarly active in reducing the growth of HeyA8 cells compared to the CD95LMUT vector.
source: This construct (containing four point mutations and confirmed to produce mRNA with no detectable full-length CD95L protein, Figure 1B) was similarly active in reducing the growth of HeyA8 cells compared to the CD95LMUT vector (Figure 1A, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 1A, left panel.

claim: CD95LMUTNP still produced truncated and likely soluble CD95L.
source: CD95LMUTNP still produced truncated and likely soluble CD95L (Figure 1B), likely due to use of an alternative start codon.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B showing a truncated protein band.

claim: The supernatant of 293T cells infected with CD95LMUTNP virus did not induce apoptosis when added to HeyA8 cells.
source: However, the supernatant of 293T cells infected with this virus did not induce apoptosis when added to HeyA8 cells (data not shown) confirming that it had no apoptosis inducing activity.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result, though the data is not shown.

claim: All three CD95L constructs (wt, MUT, MUTNP) were equally toxic to HeyA8 cells when apoptosis was suppressed with zVAD-fmk.
source: With suppressed apoptosis, all three constructs were now equally toxic to HeyA8 cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 1A, center panel.

claim: In HeyA8 CD95 k.o. cells, without the addition of zVAD-fmk, wt CD95L and CD95LMUTNP were equally active in reducing the growth of the cells.
source: In these cells, without the addition of zVAD-fmk, wt CD95L and CD95LMUTNP were again equally active in reducing the growth of the cells (Figure 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 1A, right panel.

claim: It is the CD95L mRNA that killed the cells.
source: Together, these data suggested it is the CD95L mRNA that killed the cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experiments showing toxicity independent of CD95 protein and receptor.

claim: Cell death was confirmed by quantifying nuclear fragmentation.
source: Cell death was confirmed by quantifying nuclear fragmentation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A significant increase of ROS was detected in cells expressing CD95LMUTNP.
source: We also detected a significant increase of ROS in cells expressing CD95LMUTNP (Figure 1D), which is a characteristic feature of DISE (Hadji et al., 2014; Patel and Peter, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increased ROS production is a characteristic feature of DISE.
source: We also detected a significant increase of ROS in cells expressing CD95LMUTNP (Figure 1D), which is a characteristic feature of DISE (Hadji et al., 2014; Patel and Peter, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Hadji et al., 2014; Patel and Peter, 2018).

claim: Overexpression of wild-type CD95L killed MCF-7 clone FA4 cells, which harbor a complete homozygous deletion of the entire CD95 gene.
source: Overexpression of wild-type CD95L killed clone FA4 cells, which harbor a complete homozygous deletion of the entire CD95 gene (exon 1–9), as well as CD95 protein k.o. clone #21 cells that retain some truncated mRNA expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The CD95LMUTNP (G258A) mutant construct did not produce any detectable protein.
source: This CD95LMUTNP (G258A) mutant construct did not produce any detectable protein anymore (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) but was as toxic to the CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells as CD95LMUTNP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The CD95LMUTNP (G258A) mutant was as toxic to the CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells as CD95LMUTNP.
source: This CD95LMUTNP (G258A) mutant construct did not produce any detectable protein anymore (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) but was as toxic to the CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells as CD95LMUTNP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The CD95LSIL mutant construct was equally effective in suppressing cell growth compared to two independently cloned wt CD95L constructs.
source: The activity of this mutant construct to negatively affect cell growth of CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells was compared to two independently cloned wt CD95L constructs (WT1 and WT2 in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). The mutant SIL construct was equally effective in suppressing cell growth and produced about the same amount of CD95L mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The CD95LSIL mutant produced about the same amount of CD95L mRNA as wild-type CD95L.
source: The mutant SIL construct was equally effective in suppressing cell growth and produced about the same amount of CD95L mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The CD95LSIL mutant only produced about 12% of WT CD95L protein.
source: However, the SIL construct only produced about 12% of WT CD95L protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), again supporting the observation that it is the CD95L mRNA and not the protein that elicits toxicity.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The overall predicted toxicity based on 6mer seeds was not statistically different between the WT and SIL CD95L constructs.
source: We now plotted the toxicity of all sRNAs that can be derived from either the WT or the SIL mutant CD95L and found that the overall predicted toxicity based on our toxicity screen performed in HeyA8 cells was not statistically different between the two CD95L constructs, (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is supported by the probability density plot shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Toxic sequences are embedded in the CD95LSIL ORF.
source: suggesting that toxic sequences are embedded in the CD95LSIL ORF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar toxicity despite extensive mutations.

claim: The toxicity of CD95L mRNA is a highly robust phenomenon.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that even mutating more than 300 positions in CD95L mRNA still allows it to form toxic sRNAs suggesting that the toxicity of CD95L mRNA is a highly robust phenomenon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experiments with the CD95LSIL mutant.

claim: After infection with CD95L, CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells exhibited morphological changes strikingly similar to the changes seen in wt HeyA8 cells after introduction of a CD95L-derived shRNA (shL3).
source: After infection with CD95L, CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells exhibited morphological changes strikingly similar to the changes seen in wt HeyA8 cells after introduction of a CD95L-derived shRNA (shL3) (Figure 2A, Videos 1–4) suggesting the cells died through a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by phase-contrast images shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression of CD95L caused preferential downregulation of critical survival genes and not of nonsurvival genes in a control set.
source: We found that expression of CD95L caused preferential downregulation of critical survival genes and not of nonsurvival genes in a control set (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cell death induced by CD95L mRNA resulted in a substantial loss of 11 of the 12 histones detected to be downregulated in cells treated with CD95 and CD95L-derived sh/siRNAs.
source: In addition, cell death induced by CD95L mRNA resulted in a substantial loss of 11 of the 12 histones detected to be downregulated in cells treated with CD95 and CD95L-derived sh/siRNAs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of histones is an early event during DISE.
source: Loss of histones is an early event during DISE (Putzbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Putzbach et al., 2017).

claim: Nucleosome assembly, regulation of mitosis, and genes consistent with the involvement of histones were among the most significantly downregulated RNAs across all cells in which DISE was induced.
source: A Metascape analysis demonstrated that nucleosome assembly, regulation of mitosis, and genes consistent with the involvement of histones were among the most significantly downregulated RNAs across all cells in which DISE was induced by any of the four sh/siRNAs or by the expression of CD95L mRNA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Metascape analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CD95L mRNA kills cells in the same way as CD95/L-derived si/shRNAs.
source: This suggests that CD95L mRNA kills cells in the same way as CD95/L-derived si/shRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar gene expression patterns and phenotypes.

claim: Drosha k.o. cells lacking the majority of endogenous miRNAs, but retaining expression of Ago proteins, were hypersensitive to DISE induced by si- and shRNAs.
source: Drosha k.o. cells lacking the majority of endogenous miRNAs, but retaining expression of Ago proteins, were shown to be hypersensitive to DISE induced by si- and shRNAs (Putzbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Putzbach et al., 2017).

claim: Drosha k.o. cells were hypersensitive to the expression of CD95LMUTNP.
source: Drosha k.o. cells were also hypersensitive to the expression of CD95LMUTNP (Figure 3A, p=0.014, according to a polynomial fitting model); Virtually all cells died (insert in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Toxicity elicited by CD95L was blocked following AGO2 knockdown.
source: Toxicity elicited by CD95L was blocked following AGO2 knockdown, suggesting that AGO2 was required for CD95L mRNA to be toxic.
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AGO2 was required for CD95L mRNA to be toxic.
source: Toxicity elicited by CD95L was blocked following AGO2 knockdown, suggesting that AGO2 was required for CD95L mRNA to be toxic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the AGO2 knockdown experiment shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All three CD95L versions (WT, MUTNP, SIL) killed cells with the help of the RISC.
source: This was also the case when CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells were infected with either the CD95MUTNP or the CD95SIL construct (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), confirming that all three CD95L versions killed cells with the help of the RISC.
evidence: This is supported by AGO2 knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In parental HeyA8 cells infected with CD95L WT or CD95LSIL, knockdown of AGO2 did not have any effect on cell viability.
source: As expected in these cells that died of canonical apoptosis, knockdown of AGO2 did not have any effect on cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cell death induced by CD95LMUTNP in parental HeyA8 cells was severely blunted upon AGO2 knockdown.
source: In contrast, cell death induced by CD95LMUTNP which in this experiment very efficiently killed the parental HeyA8 cells was severely blunted upon AGO2 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Large amounts of sRNAs (19-23nt in length) were detected bound to the Ago proteins in wt HCT116 cells.
source: As expected in wt HCT116 cells, large amounts of sRNAs (19-23nt in length) were detected bound to the Ago proteins (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by autoradiograph data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Both AGO1 and AGO2 were efficiently pulled down in wt HCT116 cells.
source: Both AGO1 and AGO2 were efficiently pulled down.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In Drosha k.o. cells, only a low amount of sRNAs was detected, confirming the absence of miRNAs in the RISC.
source: In contrast, in the Drosha k.o. cells, which cannot generate canonical miRNAs, only a low amount of sRNAs was detected, confirming the absence of miRNAs in the RISC.
evidence: This is supported by autoradiograph data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The amount of pulled down Ago proteins was severely reduced in Drosha k.o. cells despite comparable levels of AGO2 expression.
source: Surprisingly, the amount of pulled down Ago proteins was severely reduced despite the fact these Drosha k.o. cells express comparable levels of AGO2 (Putzbach et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and citation to prior work.

claim: The peptide did not have access to the Ago proteins in Drosha k.o. cells, presumably because it only efficiently binds to Ago proteins complexed with RNA.
source: This suggests the peptide did not have access to the Ago proteins in Drosha k.o. cells, presumably because it only efficiently binds to Ago proteins complexed with RNA as recently shown (Elkayam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation and supported by citation to Elkayam et al., 2017.

claim: In wt cells, >98.4% of Ago-bound RNAs were miRNAs.
source: The analysis of all Ago-bound RNAs showed that in the wt cells, >98.4% of bound RNAs were miRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In Drosha k.o. cells, only 34% of Ago-bound RNAs were miRNAs.
source: In contrast, only 34% of bound RNAs were miRNAs in Drosha k.o. cells (Figure 3D and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: miR-320a is processed independently of Drosha.
source: These include miRNAs that are processed independently of Drosha such as miR-320a (Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2016.

claim: miR-320a became a major RNA species bound to Ago proteins in Drosha k.o. cells.
source: Consequently, this miRNA became a major RNA species bound to Ago proteins in Drosha k.o. cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A significant increase in CD95L-derived sRNAs bound to the Ago proteins was detected in cells infected with the CD95L virus compared to cells infected with pLenti empty vector.
source: In both wt and Drosha k.o. cells, a significant increase in CD95L-derived sRNAs bound to the Ago proteins was detected in cells infected with the CD95L virus compared to cells infected with pLenti empty vector, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: CD95L-derived sRNAs corresponded to 0.0006% of all the Ago-bound RNAs in wt cells.
source: They corresponded to 0.0006% and 0.043% of all the Ago-bound RNAs in the wt cells and Drosha k.o. cells, respectively.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: CD95L-derived sRNAs corresponded to 0.043% of all the Ago-bound RNAs in Drosha k.o. cells.
source: They corresponded to 0.0006% and 0.043% of all the Ago-bound RNAs in the wt cells and Drosha k.o. cells, respectively.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Toxicity of CD95L mRNA was not due to overloading the RISC.
source: Toxicity of CD95L mRNA was, therefore, not due to overloading the RISC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low percentage of CD95L-derived sRNAs in the RISC.

claim: In the absence of most miRNAs, the total amount of RNAs bound to Ago proteins in the Drosha k.o. cells was roughly 10% of the amount bound to Ago in wt cells.
source: In the absence of most miRNAs, the total amount of RNAs bound to Ago proteins in the Drosha k.o. cells was roughly 10% of the amount bound to Ago in wt cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The reduction of Ago-bound miRNAs in Drosha k.o. cells was paralleled by a substantial increase in binding of other sRNAs to the Ago proteins.
source: The reduction of Ago-bound miRNAs in Drosha k.o. cells (Figure 3E, top row) was paralleled by a substantial increase in binding of other sRNAs to the Ago proteins (Figure 3E, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The amount of Ago-bound CD95L-derived sRNAs was >100 times higher in the Drosha k.o. cells compared to the wt cells.
source: Interestingly, the amount of Ago-bound CD95L-derived sRNAs was >100 times higher in the Drosha k.o. cells compared to the wt cells (red columns in Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Drosha k.o. cells are more sensitive to CD95L mRNA-mediated toxicity due to their ability to take up more toxic small CD95L-derived RNAs into the RISC in the absence of most miRNAs.
source: These data support our hypothesis that Drosha k.o. cells are more sensitive to CD95L mRNA-mediated toxicity due to their ability to take up more toxic small CD95L-derived RNAs into the RISC in the absence of most miRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased loading of CD95L-derived sRNAs in Drosha k.o. cells.

claim: The peak length of the most abundant Ago-bound RNA species increased from 20 to 23 nt in Drosha k.o. cells compared to wt cells.
source: Interestingly, not only did Ago proteins in Drosha k.o. cells bind much more CD95L-derived sRNAs than in the wt cells, but also the peak length of the most abundant Ago-bound RNA species increased from 20 to 23 nt (Figure 4A, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by length distribution analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 22 regions in the CD95L ORF gave rise to sRNAs that were bound by Ago proteins.
source: We identified 22 regions in the CD95L ORF that gave rise to sRNAs that were bound by Ago proteins (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by read alignment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Very similar regions of small RNAs were found in the total RNA fraction isolated from CD95LMUTNP expressing HCT116 Drosha k.o. cells.
source: To determine whether these sRNAs were formed in the cytosol and then loaded into the RISC, we also aligned all sRNAs in the total RNA fraction isolated from CD95LMUTNP expressing HCT116 Drosha k.o. cells with CD95L (Figure 4C). Interestingly, very similar regions of small RNAs were found.
evidence: This is supported by read alignment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mean and peak of the distribution of the read lengths of sRNAs bound to Ago proteins was smaller than in the total small RNAs fraction.
source: Moreover, the mean as well as the peak of the distribution of the read lengths of sRNAs bound to Ago proteins was smaller than in the total small RNAs fraction (Figure 4A, center panel), suggesting these fragments were trimmed to the appropriate length either right before they were loaded into the RISC or by the RISC itself.
evidence: This is supported by length distribution analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CD95L mRNA fragments are trimmed to the appropriate length either right before they are loaded into the RISC or by the RISC itself.
source: Moreover, the mean as well as the peak of the distribution of the read lengths of sRNAs bound to Ago proteins was smaller than in the total small RNAs fraction (Figure 4A, center panel), suggesting these fragments were trimmed to the appropriate length either right before they were loaded into the RISC or by the RISC itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the length distribution differences.

claim: Certain sRNAs were more abundant in the Ago-bound fraction when compared to total RNA relative to all other RNAs.
source: We also noticed that certain sRNAs were more abundant in the Ago-bound fraction when compared to total RNA relative to all other RNAs.
evidence: This is an observation from the RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: The general location of some of the read clusters in HeyA8 CD95 k.o. cells overlapped with the ones found in the Drosha k.o. cells.
source: While we found fewer CD95L-derived reads in these cells, the general location of some of the read clusters overlapped with the ones found in the Drosha k.o. cells and again both the mean and peak of the distribution of RNA lengths was smaller in the Ago-bound fraction versus the total RNA fraction (Figure 4A, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by read alignment analysis shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: CD95L mRNA can be processed into smaller RNA fragments, which are then trimmed to a length appropriate for incorporation into the RISC.
source: Together, these data suggest that CD95L mRNA can be processed into smaller RNA fragments, which are then trimmed to a length appropriate for incorporation into the RISC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the read length and alignment analyses.

claim: Dicer k.o. cells were still sensitive to toxicity induced by CD95L mRNA expression.
source: Dicer k.o. cells were still sensitive to toxicity induced by CD95L mRNA expression, suggesting the toxicity of the CD95L mRNA does not require the processing by either Drosha or Dicer.
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The toxicity of the CD95L mRNA does not require the processing by either Drosha or Dicer.
source: Dicer k.o. cells were still sensitive to toxicity induced by CD95L mRNA expression, suggesting the toxicity of the CD95L mRNA does not require the processing by either Drosha or Dicer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Dicer k.o. experiment shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Dicer is not involved in processing CD95L mRNA.
source: Using custom real-time qPCR primers designed to specifically detect the sRNAs from clusters 8 and 21, we detected, in both wt and Dicer k.o. cells over-expressing CD95LMUTNP, fragments from these clusters (Figure 4G), demonstrating that Dicer is not involved in processing CD95L mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The CD95L ORF mRNA forms a tightly folded structure with many of the sRNAs of the 22 clusters juxtaposing each other in stem-like structures creating regions of significant complementarity.
source: According to this analysis, the CD95L ORF mRNA forms a tightly folded structure with many of the sRNAs of the 22 clusters juxtaposing each other in stem-like structures creating regions of significant complementarity.
evidence: This is based on secondary structure prediction shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Some of the juxtaposing reads were found in duplex structures with 3' overhangs.
source: Interestingly, some of the juxtaposing reads were found in duplex structures with 3' overhangs.
evidence: This is based on secondary structure prediction shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three oligonucleotides derived from clusters 7, 15 and 22, when expressed as siRNAs, were toxic to HeyA8, H460, M565 and 3LL cells.
source: Three of these oligonucleotides (derived from clusters 7, 15 and 22) when expressed as siRNAs were toxic to HeyA8, H460, M565 and 3LL cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only the 5' fragment of CD95L caused a small reduction in cell growth when compared to full length CD95L in CD95 k.o. HeyA8 cells.
source: Only the 5' fragment caused a small reduction in cell growth when compared to full length CD95L (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In the hypersensitive Drosha k.o. HCT116 cells, both CD95L fragments showed weak toxicity.
source: While neither of the two fragments were toxic to wt HCT116 cells, in the hypersensitive Drosha k.o. HCT116 cells both fragments showed weak toxicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Fragments of CD95L show reduced toxicity which could be due to their lower expression levels and/or their inability to properly fold and form sRNAs.
source: These data suggest that fragments of CD95L show reduced toxicity which could be due to their lower expression levels and/or their inability to properly fold and form sRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fragment experiments.

claim: 558 (~10%) of genes with Ago bound reads were protein coding genes that met the criteria for processing.
source: We found Ago bound reads of 10 or more reads/location that aligned with 5629 genes in the human genome. Of these genes ~ 10% were noncoding, 558 (~10%) were protein coding genes that met our criteria for processing, and 4498 genes (~80%) were protein coding genes that did not.
evidence: This is based on analysis of Ago pull-down RNA-Seq data.

claim: In almost all cases, similar to processed CD95L, the average length of the reads bound to the Ago proteins was smaller than the ones found in total RNA.
source: In almost all cases, similar to processed CD95L, the average length of the reads bound to the Ago proteins was smaller than the ones found in total RNA (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by length distribution analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The reads derived from processed genes were between 5–10 times more abundant in the RISC of cells devoid of Drosha expression.
source: When all small reads derived from these five genes were aligned with the human genome, we observed that: 1) The reads were between 5–10 times more abundant in the RISC of cells devoid of Drosha expression
evidence: This is supported by genome alignment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The processed gene reads were loaded equally efficiently in cells expressing the empty vector control or the CD95L expressing virus.
source: and 2) they were loaded equally efficiently in cells expressing the empty vector control or the CD95L expressing virus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by genome alignment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes found in many of the enriched clusters were involved in cell growth.
source: Strikingly, genes found in many of these enriched clusters were involved in cell growth (green rows in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by DAVID GO analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The most significantly enriched genes were involved in protein translation.
source: In fact, the most significantly enriched genes were involved in protein translation (dark green rows in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by DAVID GO analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: 38 of the mRNAs of the 50 ribosomal proteins (76%) in the analysis were processed and loaded into the RISC.
source: Interestingly, in addition to cyclin D1, MYC (Figure 5B) and CDK6 (Supplementary File 1) and many initiation and elongation factors, 38 of the mRNAs of the 50 ribosomal proteins (76%) in the analysis were processed in this way (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Proteins involved in protein translation may be marked to be processed and loaded into the RISC.
source: This suggests that proteins involved in protein translation may be marked to be processed and loaded into the RISC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of translation-related genes.

claim: Drosha k.o. cells consistently grew slower than their parental wt cells.
source: We noticed that Drosha k.o. cells consistently grew slower than their parental wt cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Most RISC bound sRNAs in wt cells were miRNAs with low seed toxicity.
source: Most RISC bound sRNAs in wt cells were miRNAs with low seed toxicity (blue columns in Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by seed toxicity analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In Drosha k.o. cells the majority of RISC bound sRNAs had a rather toxic 6mer seed.
source: In contrast, in Drosha k.o. cells the majority of RISC bound sRNAs had a rather toxic 6mer seed (red columns in Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by seed toxicity analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Knockdown of AGO2 in Drosha k.o. cells resulted in an increase of their growth rate that was similar to the one observed in wt cells.
source: To test this, we knocked down AGO2 in the Drosha k.o. cells and this treatment resulted in an increase of their growth rate that was now similar to the one observed in wt cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by cell confluence data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Endogenous RISC bound sRNAs may regulate cell growth through the DISE mechanism.
source: These data suggest that endogenous RISC bound sRNAs may regulate cell growth through the DISE mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the AGO2 knockdown experiment in Drosha k.o. cells.

claim: The CD95L mRNA is processed into sRNAs that are loaded into the RISC that then target critical survival genes.
source: In summary, our data suggest that si- and/or shRNAs with certain seed sequences present in CD95 and CD95L and the entire CD95L ORF are toxic to cancer cells. The CD95L mRNA is processed into sRNAs that are loaded into the RISC that then target critical survival genes.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cell death from CD95L mRNA occurs largely through 6mer seed toxicity.
source: This results in cell death largely through 6mer seed toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation with 6mer seed toxicity and the mechanism of DISE.

claim: A high miRNA content, by 'filling up' the RISC, might render cells less sensitive to this form of cell death.
source: Furthermore, our data suggest that a high miRNA content, by 'filling up' the RISC, might render cells less sensitive to this form of cell death
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential sensitivity of wt vs Drosha k.o. cells.

claim: Multiple endogenous mRNAs are processed and loaded into the RISC and may regulate cell fate.
source: and that multiple endogenous mRNAs are processed and loaded into the RISC and may regulate cell fate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of endogenous genes in the RISC shown in Figure 5.

claim: Previous studies showed transgenic expression of CD95L using viruses killed multiple cancer cells that were completely resistant to CD95 mediated apoptosis.
source: This is intriguing considering that previous studies showed transgenic expression of CD95L using viruses killed multiple cancer cells that were completely resistant to CD95 mediated apoptosis (ElOjeimy et al., 2006; Hyer et al., 2000; Sudarshan et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Both the CD95L protein and mRNA are toxic to cells through distinct mechanisms.
source: However, we now provide an alternate explanation—namely, both the CD95L protein and mRNA are toxic to cells through distinct mechanisms. The protein induces apoptosis, and the mRNA induces toxicity through an RNAi-based mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings in the manuscript.

claim: There are several candidate RNases that are capable of processing mRNAs.
source: We demonstrate that Dicer and Drosha are not involved in generating the Ago-bound CD95L-derived fragments but there are several candidate RNases that are capable of processing mRNAs.
evidence: This is general knowledge about RNA processing.

claim: It is likely that CD95L-derived fragment intermediates are incorporated into the RISC and then trimmed to the appropriate length by Ago.
source: Given the differences in length distribution between the cytosolic versus Ago-bound RNA fragments, it is likely that CD95L-derived fragment intermediates are incorporated into the RISC and then trimmed to the appropriate length by Ago.
evidence: This is an inference based on the length distribution data.

claim: A similar mechanism occurs during the maturation of the erythropoietic miR-451, where the pre-miRNA is first cleaved by AGO2 and then trimmed at the 3' end to the final mature form by the exoribonuclease PARN.
source: Indeed, a similar mechanism is known to occur during the maturation of the erythropoietic miR-451, where the pre-miRNA is first cleaved by AGO2 and then trimmed at the 3' end to the final mature form by the exoribonuclease PARN (Yoda et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoda et al., 2013.

claim: A similar process occurs with agotrons, which consist of an excised intron loaded into the RISC in a manner independent of Drosha or Dicer pre-processing.
source: Furthermore, a similar process occurs with the recently identified class of Ago-bound RNAs called agotrons (Hansen et al., 2016), which consist of an excised intron loaded into the RISC in a manner independent of Drosha or Dicer pre-processing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2016.

claim: This is the first evidence of an overexpressed cDNA exerting toxicity via an RNAi-dependent mechanism in mammalian cells.
source: Our data provide the first evidence of an overexpressed cDNA exerting toxicity via an RNAi-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: It was first shown in plants that overexpressed transgenes can be converted into RNAi active short RNA sequences.
source: It was first shown in plants that overexpressed transgenes can be converted into RNAi active short RNA sequences (Hamilton and Baulcombe, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hamilton and Baulcombe, 1999.

claim: The CD95L-derived sRNAs will likely act in a miRNA-like fashion by targeting 3'UTRs of survival genes through 6mer seed toxicity.
source: The CD95L-derived sRNAs will likely act in a miRNA-like fashion by targeting 3'UTRs of survival genes through 6mer seed toxicity (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of 6mer seed toxicity described in prior work.

claim: CAG-repeat-containing mRNAs have been shown to induce sRNA formation and cellular toxicity via RNAi.
source: CAG-repeat-containing mRNAs have been shown to induce sRNA formation and cellular toxicity via RNAi (Bañez-Coronel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bañez-Coronel et al., 2012.

claim: sCAGs likely target fully complementary CUG containing repeat regions in the ORFs of genes critical for cell survival in an siRNA-like mechanism.
source: However, we recently reported that these sCAGs likely target fully complementary CUG containing repeat regions in the ORFs of genes critical for cell survival in an siRNA-like mechanism (Murmann et al., 2018a; Murmann et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Small mRNA-derived RNAs have been reported to be bound to all four Ago proteins before.
source: Small mRNA-derived RNAs have been reported to be bound to all four Ago proteins before (Burroughs et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burroughs et al., 2011.

claim: In cells with disabled miRNA processing, about 3% of the protein coding genes can be processed and loaded into the RISC.
source: In contrast, we now show that in cells with disabled miRNA processing, about 3% of the the protein coding genes can be processed in this way
evidence: This is based on the analysis of Ago-bound reads from protein coding genes.

claim: These processed genes are strongly enriched in GO terms associated with protein translation (initiation and elongation) as well as with cell cycle regulation and cell proliferation.
source: and that these genes are strongly enriched in GO terms associated with protein translation (initiation and elongation) as well as with cell cycle regulation and cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The findings may be relevant for situations in which cellular miRNA levels are low, such as in somatic stem cells or in advanced cancers.
source: Our findings may be relevant for situations in which cellular miRNA levels are low, such as in somatic stem cells (Morin et al., 2008) or in advanced cancers which are characterized by a global downregulation of miRNAs (Lu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is speculation about the biological relevance, supported by citations.

claim: Upregulation of CD95L has been noticed in multiple stress-related conditions such as after treatment with chemotherapy.
source: We and others have noticed upregulation of CD95L in multiple stress-related conditions such as after treatment with chemotherapy ((Friesen et al., 1999) and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by citation and unpublished observations.

claim: It is unlikely CD95L is the only gene whose mRNA is toxic to cells.
source: It is unlikely CD95L is the only gene whose mRNA is toxic to cells, as this mRNA-based level of toxicity would be redundant with the potent killing capacity of the CD95L protein.
evidence: This is speculation based on biological reasoning.

claim: Nature likely distributed this mRNA-based toxicity-inducing capacity over many genes in the genome to prevent activating it when any one of those genes is upregulated during specific cellular processes.
source: Therefore, nature likely distributed this mRNA-based toxicity-inducing capacity over many genes in the genome to prevent activating it when any one of those genes is upregulated during specific cellular processes.
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary design.

claim: There exists an entire network of genes that can release toxic sRNAs when the appropriate stimulus is encountered.
source: It is more likely there exists an entire network of these genes that can release toxic sRNAs when the appropriate stimulus is encountered.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Other genes have been identified that contain sequences that when converted to shRNAs kill cancer cells through 6mer seed toxicity.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis we recently identified other genes that contain sequences that when converted to shRNAs kill cancer cells through 6mer seed toxicity (Patel and Peter, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.
